claim: Human protein kinases evolved from a few protein kinases in unicellular organisms, with more than 500 human protein kinases existing.
source: The evolution of more than 500 human protein kinases from a few protein kinases in unicellular organisms allowed for the development of complexity via differential regulation (Manning et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manning et al., 2002.

claim: Autophosphorylation of T288 in the activation loop increases the catalytic activity of Aurora A.
source: Autophosphorylation of T288 in the activation loop increases the catalytic activity of Aurora A (Walter et al., 2000; Littlepage et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Walter et al., 2000 and Littlepage et al., 2002.

claim: Intramolecular autophosphorylation has recently been suggested for Aurora A and Chk2 based on indirect kinetic measurements.
source: Intramolecular autophosphorylation has recently been suggested for Aurora A and Chk2 based on indirect kinetic measurements (Dodson et al., 2013) adding to the controversy by disagreeing with the intermolecular mechanism proposed for other protein kinases (Oliver et al., 2006, 2007; Pike et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dodson et al., 2013 and other references.

claim: TPX2-bound Aurora A at the spindle microtubules is dephosphorylated at T288 during mitosis in vivo.
source: It was shown that in vivo during mitosis, TPX2-bound Aurora A at the spindle microtubules is dephosphorylated at the crucial T288 (Toya et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Toya et al., 2011.

claim: T288-dephosphorylated Aurora A exhibits very low kinase activity.
source: Since T288-dephosphorylated Aurora A exhibits very low kinase activity, a second kinase-independent function of Aurora A was postulated (Littlepage, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Littlepage, 2002.

claim: Escherichia coli-produced kinases are heavily phosphorylated due to autophosphorylation and phosphorylation by E. coli kinases during expression.
source: Part of the difficulty consists in obtaining a dephosphorylated protein, since Escherichia coli-produced kinases are heavily phosphorylated due to autophosphorylation and phosphorylation by E. coli kinases during expression (Enami and Ishihama, 1984) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Enami and Ishihama, 1984 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Dephosphorylated Aurora A was obtained after treatment of heavily phosphorylated, Escherichia coli-produced Aurora A with λ-protein phosphatase (λPP).
source: The dephosphorylated protein was obtained after treatment of heavily phosphorylated, Escherichia coli-produced Aurora A with λ-protein phosphatase (λPP).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used to obtain dephosphorylated Aurora A, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Phosphorylated Aurora A catalyzes AP phosphorylation with a kcat of 1.0 ± 0.2 s−1.
source: Phosphorylated Aurora A catalyzes AP phosphorylation 100-fold faster than the dephosphorylated kinase (1.0 ± 0.2 s−1 vs 0.01 ± 0.005 s—1; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Dephosphorylated Aurora A catalyzes AP phosphorylation with a kcat of 0.01 ± 0.005 s−1.
source: Phosphorylated Aurora A catalyzes AP phosphorylation 100-fold faster than the dephosphorylated kinase (1.0 ± 0.2 s−1 vs 0.01 ± 0.005 s—1; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Phosphorylated Aurora A catalyzes AP phosphorylation 100-fold faster than dephosphorylated Aurora A.
source: Phosphorylated Aurora A catalyzes AP phosphorylation 100-fold faster than the dephosphorylated kinase (1.0 ± 0.2 s−1 vs 0.01 ± 0.005 s—1; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Aurora A T288V mutant shows comparable low activity to dephosphorylated Aurora A with kcatAP = 0.05 ± 0.002 s−1.
source: This mutant shows comparable low activity to the dephosphorylated kinase (kcatAP = 0.05 ± 0.002 s−1) serving as a control for quantifying the rate acceleration provided by T288 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on the T288V mutant.

claim: TPX21−45 stimulates AP phosphorylation by 50-fold for dephosphorylated Aurora A.
source: Our data suggest the first scenario since AP phosphorylation is stimulated by 50- and 25-fold by TPX21−45 for the dephosphorylated Aurora A and T288V Aurora A, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: TPX21−45 stimulates AP phosphorylation by 25-fold for T288V Aurora A.
source: Our data suggest the first scenario since AP phosphorylation is stimulated by 50- and 25-fold by TPX21−45 for the dephosphorylated Aurora A and T288V Aurora A, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The rates of dephosphorylated Aurora A plus TPX21−45 are comparable to that of phosphorylated Aurora A alone.
source: The rates of dephosphorylated Aurora A plus TPX21−45 are comparable to that of phosphorylated Aurora A alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing the rates.

claim: Addition of TPX2 to phosphorylated Aurora A results in only a twofold increase in kcat.
source: Addition of TPX2 to phosphorylated Aurora A results in only a twofold increase in kcat.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on the effect of TPX2 on phosphorylated Aurora A.

claim: The crystal structure of dephosphorylated Aurora A in the absence of TPX21−45 and bound to AMPPCP is monomeric and in an inactive conformation.
source: The AMPPCP-bound, dephosphorylated Aurora A is monomeric and in an inactive conformation, similar to previously solved structures of the same protein bound to adenosine (PDB ID 1MUO [Cheetham et al., 2002]) or AMPPNP (PDB ID 2C6D [Heron et al., 2006]).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data and comparison to previously solved structures.

claim: The TPX2-bound Aurora A structure reveals a dimer made by two molecules of Aurora A, TPX2, and AMPPCP in the asymmetric unit.
source: In contrast, the TPX2-bound Aurora A structure reveals a dimer made by two molecules of Aurora A, TPX2, and AMPPCP in the asymmetric unit (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Both monomers in the TPX2-bound dephosphorylated Aurora A dimer are in an active conformation despite being dephosphorylated.
source: Interestingly, both monomers are in an active conformation despite being dephosphorylated (Figure 2C), a feature that has never been seen before in Aurora kinases.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Binding of TPX2 causes a slight rotation of the αC-helix towards the catalytic center, allowing for the conserved E181-K162 ion pair to form.
source: First, binding of TPX2 causes a slight rotation of the αC-helix towards the catalytic center, thus allowing for the conserved, stabilizing E181-K162 ion pair to form.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of the TPX2-bound Aurora A structure.

claim: The αC-helix rotation results in movement of F275 of the conserved DFG motif from the DFG-out into the DFG-in position.
source: The αC-helix rotation also results in movement of F275 of the conserved DFG motif from the DFG-out into the DFG-in position (Martin et al., 2012) (Figure 2C, bottom inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 2C and a citation to Martin et al., 2012.

claim: Movement of F275 positions the catalytic D274 in the correct orientation to carry out phosphoryl transfer.
source: This positions the catalytic D274 in the correct orientation to carry out phosphoryl transfer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural analysis of the TPX2-bound Aurora A structure.

claim: Movement of F275 initiates a cascade of side chain interactions that result in the completion of the regulatory spine (R-spine).
source: Second, movement of F275 initiates a cascade of side chain interactions that result in the completion of the regulatory spine originating from the αF-helix (R-spine; Figure 2C, bottom inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Identification of the completed R-spine is based on the Local Spatial Patterns (LSP) alignment, a bioinformatics tool developed by the Taylor laboratory.
source: Identification of the completed R-spine, a hallmark of an active kinase, is based on the Local Spatial Patterns (LSP) alignment, a bioinformatics tool developed by the Taylor laboratory (Kornev et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kornev et al., 2008.

claim: Aurora A, despite being dephosphorylated, is in an active conformation when bound to TPX2.
source: From these structural features it appears that Aurora A, despite being dephosphorylated, is in an active conformation when bound to TPX2.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of the TPX2-bound dephosphorylated Aurora A structure.

claim: Formation of the β6/β9 antiparallel β sheets prime the MgATP for catalysis in active Aurora A.
source: The final signatures for an active state Ser/Thr kinase involve changes around the activation segment. Formation of the β6/β9 antiparallel β sheets, that are not present in the inactive kinase, prime the MgATP for catalysis together with the other conformational changes described above.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of active Aurora A.

claim: The correct positioning of D256 for activating the hydroxyl of the substrate in active Aurora A is achieved by a hydrogen bond network to T292, which in turn H-bonds to K258.
source: Finally, the correct positioning of D256 for activating the hydroxyl of the substrate in active Aurora A is achieved by a hydrogen bond network to T292, which in turn H-bonds to K258 with distances shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The structural features for active Aurora A are fully conserved among eukaryotic Ser/Thr kinases.
source: All these features are fully conserved among eukaryotic Ser/Thr kinases (Nolen and Taylor, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nolen and Taylor, 2004.

claim: In the presence of TPX21−45, the N-terminal anchor point of the activation loop (β6 and β9 sheets) is present in both monomers.
source: Left: in the presence of TPX21−45, the N-terminal (β6 and β9 sheets) anchor point of the activation loop is present in both monomers whereas the C-terminal H-bond contacts typical for a fully active kinase (between D256/K258 and T292-OH) are only visible for the enzyme monomer in red, which we therefore define as the enzyme molecule.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The C-terminal H-bond contacts typical for a fully active kinase (between D256/K258 and T292-OH) are only visible for the enzyme monomer in the TPX2-bound dimer.
source: Left: in the presence of TPX21−45, the N-terminal (β6 and β9 sheets) anchor point of the activation loop is present in both monomers whereas the C-terminal H-bond contacts typical for a fully active kinase (between D256/K258 and T292-OH) are only visible for the enzyme monomer in red, which we therefore define as the enzyme molecule.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: In the absence of TPX21−45, the N- and C-terminal anchor points are not present and the protein is in an inactive state.
source: Right: for comparison, in the absence of TPX21−45, the N- and C-terminal anchor points are not present and the protein is in an inactive state.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: W313 in monomeric Aurora A typically interacts with P297 and P298.
source: In the C-lobe, W313 that would typically interact with P297 and P298 in monomeric Aurora A, now interacts with the identical Pro residues of the other Aurora A monomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of monomeric Aurora A.

claim: In the TPX2-bound dimer, W313 interacts with P297 and P298 of the other Aurora A monomer.
source: In the C-lobe, W313 that would typically interact with P297 and P298 in monomeric Aurora A, now interacts with the identical Pro residues of the other Aurora A monomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis of the TPX2-bound dimer.

claim: The E299–R371 salt bridge is domain swapped in the TPX2-bound Aurora A dimer.
source: Lastly, the E299–R371 salt bridge is also domain swapped (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Trans-activation through domain-swapped dimers has been proposed for a number of kinases.
source: While trans-activation through domain-swapped dimers seen in X-ray structures has been proposed for a number of kinases (Figure 3–figure supplement 1) (Oliver et al., 2006, 2007; Pike et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009), a recent report on Aurora A and Chk2 suggesting a strict intramolecular autophosphorylation of the activation segment for both enzymes has fueled controversy on this topic (Dodson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oliver et al., 2006, 2007; Pike et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009 and reference to Figure 3–figure supplement 1.

claim: A recent report suggests strict intramolecular autophosphorylation of the activation segment for Aurora A and Chk2.
source: While trans-activation through domain-swapped dimers seen in X-ray structures has been proposed for a number of kinases (Figure 3–figure supplement 1) (Oliver et al., 2006, 2007; Pike et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009), a recent report on Aurora A and Chk2 suggesting a strict intramolecular autophosphorylation of the activation segment for both enzymes has fueled controversy on this topic (Dodson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dodson et al., 2013.

claim: The asymmetric dimer within the unit cell has monomer I showing complete electron density for the activation segment while monomer II is missing residues 283–288.
source: In contrast we find an asymmetric dimer within the unit cell with monomer I showing complete electron density for the activation segment while monomer II is missing residues 283–288 (Figure 2B, red and blue, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Only monomer I has the perfect geometry of the conserved hydrogen bond network found in a catalytically prone kinase between residues D256, K258, and T292.
source: In addition, only monomer I has the perfect geometry of the conserved hydrogen bond network found in a catalytically prone kinase between residues D256, K258, and T292 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Monomer I may be the enzyme molecule recognizing monomer II as its substrate.
source: Therefore we speculated that monomer I may be the enzyme molecule recognizing monomer II as its substrate.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on structural analysis.

claim: Only T288 of monomer II with a more flexible activation loop segment can be rearranged at a close distance to the γ-phosphate of AMPPCP without displacing the AMPPCP from its original position.
source: Only T288 of monomer II (proposed as the substrate molecule above) with a more flexible activation loop segment can be rearranged at a close distance to the γ-phosphate of AMPPCP without displacing the AMPPCP from its original position (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted MD simulations presented in Figure 3B.

claim: A significant amount of dimer was detected for Aurora A by SAXS and AUC experiments.
source: A significant amount of dimer was detected for Aurora A and the relative concentration was independent of the presence of TPX2.
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS and AUC experimental data.

claim: The relative concentration of Aurora A dimer was independent of the presence of TPX2.
source: A significant amount of dimer was detected for Aurora A and the relative concentration was independent of the presence of TPX2.
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS and AUC experimental data.

claim: Separate peaks for the dimer and monomer were observed in a sedimentation velocity run, revealing a slow interconversion rate between dimer and monomer.
source: Importantly, the fact that separate peaks for the dimer and monomer were observed in a sedimentation velocity run reveals a slow interconversion rate between dimer and monomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by AUC experimental data.

claim: Fitting of the SAXS data required inclusion of 9% dimer of the shape of the X-ray structure.
source: Fitting of the SAXS data required inclusion of 9% dimer of the shape of our X-ray structure, supporting the notion that the swapped dimer seen in X-ray crystallography exists in solution in agreement with the AUC data.
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS experimental data.

claim: The KD for Aurora A dimer formation is estimated to be above 300 μM.
source: Protein solubility prohibited determination of the KD, but from both the concentration dependence observed in AUC as well as SAXS experiments one can estimate that the KD is above 300 μM.
evidence: The claim is an estimate based on AUC and SAXS experimental data.

claim: Aurora A D274A is a kinase-impaired version that is unable to autophosphorylate within the reaction time frame.
source: D274A is a kinase-impaired version (Wan et al., 2008) that is unable to autophosphorylate within our reaction time frame (Figure 5A, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A and a citation to Wan et al., 2008.

claim: Equal concentrations of dephosphorylated wild type Aurora A122−403 and Aurora A125−392 D274A lead to comparable phosphorylation rates for both proteins, demonstrating an intermolecular autophosphorylation mechanism for Aurora A.
source: While Aurora A125−392 D274A cannot phosphorylate itself, equal concentrations of dephosphorylated wild type Aurora A122−403 and Aurora A125−392 D274A lead to comparable phosphorylation rates for both proteins, demonstrating an intermolecular autophosphorylation mechanism for Aurora A (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Much faster autophosphorylation kinetics are observed when 1 μM Aurora A is diluted from a 200 μM stock solution compared to a 20 μM stock solution.
source: The rate of autophosphorylation was measured for samples of 1 μM Aurora A prepared by dilution from 200 μM and 20 μM stock solutions. Although the final protein concentration in both samples is the same, much faster autophosphorylation was detected for the sample diluted from the more highly concentrated stock solution (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The sample diluted from the more highly concentrated stock solution contains a higher concentration of the slowly dissociating dimer.
source: Since the latter sample contains a higher concentration of this slowly dissociating dimer, this experiment directly demonstrates dimer-dependent autophosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on dilution experiments.

claim: The dilution experiment directly demonstrates dimer-dependent autophosphorylation.
source: Since the latter sample contains a higher concentration of this slowly dissociating dimer, this experiment directly demonstrates dimer-dependent autophosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on dilution experiments.

claim: TPX2 strongly accelerates autophosphorylation.
source: TPX2 strongly accelerates autophosphorylation, in agreement with previous reports (Eyers et al., 2003), and as seen for peptide phosphorylation (Figure 1B and Figure 1–figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Eyers et al., 2003.

claim: Intermolecular autophosphorylation proceeds via the long-lived swapped dimer.
source: Notably, this intermolecular autophosphorylation again proceeds via the long-lived swapped dimer (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The dimer is necessary but not sufficient for autophosphorylation.
source: We note that although necessary, the dimer is not sufficient for autophosphorylation, because the catalytically impaired D274A mutant shows a high percentage of dimer (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: TPX2 triggers a conformational change that results in a catalytically active dimer.
source: Clearly, TPX2 triggers a conformational change that results in a catalytically active dimer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on TPX2's effect on Aurora A.

claim: C290 of one monomer contacts Y334 of the αG-helix of the other monomer in the TPX2-bound dimer.
source: We rationalized that a C290A mutation could work because C290 of one monomer contacts Y334 of the αG-helix of the other monomer, while in phosphorylated monomeric Aurora A, C290 contacts K143, W277, L289, and G291 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 6A,B.

claim: In phosphorylated monomeric Aurora A, C290 contacts K143, W277, L289, and G291.
source: We rationalized that a C290A mutation could work because C290 of one monomer contacts Y334 of the αG-helix of the other monomer, while in phosphorylated monomeric Aurora A, C290 contacts K143, W277, L289, and G291 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis presented in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The C290A mutation results in a primarily monomeric form.
source: The C290A mutation indeed results in a primarily monomeric form (Figure 6C) that also has severely impaired autophosphorylation activity (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The C290A mutation has severely impaired autophosphorylation activity.
source: The C290A mutation indeed results in a primarily monomeric form (Figure 6C) that also has severely impaired autophosphorylation activity (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Once phosphorylated, C290A has nearly normal catalytic activity towards the AP substrate.
source: However, once phosphorylated, C290A has nearly normal catalytic activity towards the AP substrate (Figure 6E), buttressing the functional role of the swapped WT dimer for autophosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: In a 1:1 mixture of dephosphorylated WT and C290A mutant, WT autophosphorylation precedes C290A phosphorylation in the early reaction time course.
source: Particularly striking is the observation that in a 1:1 mixture of dephosphorylated WT and C290A mutant, WT autophosphorylation precedes C290A phosphorylation in the early reaction time course (Figure 6D, right and inset) but phosphorylation kinetics are identical at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Phosphorylation kinetics are identical at later time points for WT and C290A in a 1:1 mixture.
source: Particularly striking is the observation that in a 1:1 mixture of dephosphorylated WT and C290A mutant, WT autophosphorylation precedes C290A phosphorylation in the early reaction time course (Figure 6D, right and inset) but phosphorylation kinetics are identical at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: The C290A mutant is incapable of forming a hybrid swapped dimer between one molecule each of dephosphorylated C290A and WT protein.
source: The C290A mutant is incapable of forming a hybrid swapped dimer between one molecule each of dephosphorylated C290A and WT protein, explaining the lag in its phosphorylation kinetics relative to WT.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on the C290A mutant.

claim: TPX21−43 had been identified as essential for Aurora A activation and protection from PP1, PP2A, or λPP-directed dephosphorylation.
source: TPX21−43 had been identified as essential for Aurora A activation and protection from PP1, PP2A, or λPP-directed dephosphorylation (Eyers et al., 2003; Tsai et al., 2003; Satinover et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eyers et al., 2003; Tsai et al., 2003; Satinover et al., 2004.

claim: In the X-ray structure of TPX21−43 bound to phosphorylated Aurora A, TPX26−23 was seen in an extended conformation.
source: This finding was further substantiated by an X-ray structure of TPX21−43 bound to phosphorylated Aurora A (Bayliss et al., 2003) (Figure 7–figure supplement 1). In this structure, TPX26−23 was seen in an extended conformation, whereas TPX230−43 formed a regular helix that was proposed to be crucial in protecting Aurora A from phosphatase-mediated T288 dephosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bayliss et al., 2003 and reference to Figure 7–figure supplement 1.

claim: TPX230−43 formed a regular helix that was proposed to be crucial in protecting Aurora A from phosphatase-mediated T288 dephosphorylation.
source: This finding was further substantiated by an X-ray structure of TPX21−43 bound to phosphorylated Aurora A (Bayliss et al., 2003) (Figure 7–figure supplement 1). In this structure, TPX26−23 was seen in an extended conformation, whereas TPX230−43 formed a regular helix that was proposed to be crucial in protecting Aurora A from phosphatase-mediated T288 dephosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bayliss et al., 2003 and reference to Figure 7–figure supplement 1.

claim: In the dimer structure, only TPX24/6−20/22 could be visualized, and the previously seen helical part was completely missing.
source: Surprisingly, in our dimer structure, we could only visualize TPX24/6−20/22 (Figure 2A,B and Figure 7–figure supplement 1), and the previously seen helical part was completely missing.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 2A,B and Figure 7–figure supplement 1.

claim: TPX21−25 bound to Aurora A with the same affinity as longer versions (TPX21−147 or TPX21−45).
source: First, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) showed that TPX21−25 bound to Aurora A with the same affinity as longer versions (TPX21−147 or TPX21−45) and did not discriminate between the phosphorylated and dephosphorylated states of the protein (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: TPX21−25 did not discriminate between the phosphorylated and dephosphorylated states of Aurora A.
source: First, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) showed that TPX21−25 bound to Aurora A with the same affinity as longer versions (TPX21−147 or TPX21−45) and did not discriminate between the phosphorylated and dephosphorylated states of the protein (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: No signal was detected for TPX225−45 with Aurora A in ITC.
source: On the other hand, no signal was detected for TPX225−45 with Aurora A in ITC.
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: TPX21−25 binding could trigger an increase in activity of dephosphorylated Aurora A towards peptides and autophosphorylation.
source: Second, TPX21−25 binding could trigger an increase in activity of dephosphorylated Aurora A towards peptides and autophosphorylation (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (not shown).

claim: TPX225−45 had no effect on Aurora A activity.
source: In contrast, TPX225−45 had no effect on Aurora A activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: TPX21−25 could protect Aurora A from λPP-directed dephosphorylation as well as TPX21−45.
source: Third, TPX21−25 could protect Aurora A from λPP-directed dephosphorylation as well as TPX21−45, whereas no protection was found for TPX225−45 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: No protection from λPP-directed dephosphorylation was found for TPX225−45.
source: Third, TPX21−25 could protect Aurora A from λPP-directed dephosphorylation as well as TPX21−45, whereas no protection was found for TPX225−45 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The first 25 amino acids of TPX2 are primarily responsible for both activation of the enzyme and protection from dephosphorylation.
source: These functional data suggest that the first 25 amino acids of TPX2 are primarily responsible for both activation of the enzyme and protection from dephosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from functional data on TPX2 fragments.

claim: The specific interaction between a hydrophobic groove at the junction of the αB/αC-helices in the N-lobe of kinases and a short sequence called 'the hydrophobic motif' (Tyr/Phe-X(X)-Tyr/Phe) seems to be a conserved regulatory mechanism across the AGC family.
source: This specific interaction between a hydrophobic groove at the junction of the αB/αC-helices in the N-lobe of kinases and a short sequence called 'the hydrophobic motif' (Tyr/Phe-X(X)-Tyr/Phe) from either another partner or from its own C-terminal tail, seems to be a conserved regulatory mechanism across the AGC family (Figure 7–figure supplement 2) (Zhang et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 1994 and reference to Figure 7–figure supplement 2.

claim: For CMGC kinases, the hydrophobic groove is occupied by activating cyclin proteins.
source: For CMGC kinases, the hydrophobic groove is occupied by activating cyclin proteins, as originally reported for cyclin binding to the N-lobe of Cdk2 which leads to reorientation of the activation loop and αC-helix into an active conformation (Jeffrey et al., 1995) similar to the effect of TPX2 on Aurora A.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jeffrey et al., 1995.

claim: Cyclin binding to the N-lobe of Cdk2 leads to reorientation of the activation loop and αC-helix into an active conformation.
source: For CMGC kinases, the hydrophobic groove is occupied by activating cyclin proteins, as originally reported for cyclin binding to the N-lobe of Cdk2 which leads to reorientation of the activation loop and αC-helix into an active conformation (Jeffrey et al., 1995) similar to the effect of TPX2 on Aurora A.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jeffrey et al., 1995.

claim: In MAPK, activity is increased by binding of the proteins' own C-terminal tails into the hydrophobic groove.
source: In MAPK, activity is increased by binding of the proteins' own C-terminal tails into this hydrophobic groove (Baumli et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baumli et al., 2008.

claim: In the tyrosine kinase (TK) family, an N-terminal fragment that precedes the kinase domain of c-KIT, MET, and Ephrin nestles inside the hydrophobic pocket, and autoinhibits the kinases.
source: In the tyrosine kinase (TK) family, an N-terminal fragment that precedes the kinase domain of c-KIT, MET, and Ephrin nestles inside the hydrophobic pocket, and autoinhibits the kinases (Chan et al., 2003; Mol et al., 2003, 2004; Davis et al., 2008; Eathiraj et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2003; Mol et al., 2003, 2004; Davis et al., 2008; Eathiraj et al., 2011.

claim: In the EGFR members of the TK family, the hydrophobic motif is used as a docking point for kinase activation through dimerization.
source: In the EGFR members of the TK family, this hydrophobic motif is used as a docking point for kinase activation through dimerization (Zhang et al., 2006; Jura et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2006; Jura et al., 2011.

claim: Y8 and Y10 of TPX2 nestled inside the hydrophobic αB/αC pocket in Aurora A are likely the key triggers for kinase activation.
source: This striking conservation of a very specific recognition mechanism across evolutionarily divergent kinase families suggests that Y8 and Y10 of TPX2 nestled inside the hydrophobic αB/αC pocket in Aurora A are likely the key triggers for kinase activation (Figure 7–figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural analysis and comparison across kinase families, as shown in Figure 7–figure supplement 2.

claim: The combined biochemical, thermodynamic, structural, and computational data resolve the controversy about the molecular mechanism(s) of autophosphorylation in Aurora A by directly measuring the process of autophosphorylation and linking it to a long-lived functional dimer of dephosphorylated Aurora A.
source: Our combined biochemical, thermodynamic, structural, and computational data resolve the controversy about the molecular mechanism(s) of autophosphorylation in Aurora A by directly measuring the process of autophosphorylation and linking it to a long-lived functional dimer of dephosphorylated Aurora A.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The mechanism of intramolecular autophosphorylation put forward by Dodson et al. (2013) is based on measuring the kinetics of peptide phosphorylation using an automated microchip assay as indirect readout, and not by monitoring autophosphorylation.
source: This is in sharp contrast to the mechanism of intramolecular autophosphorylation put forward by Dodson et al. (2013) based on measuring the kinetics of peptide phosphorylation using an automated microchip assay as indirect readout, and not by monitoring autophosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is a critique of the methodology used by Dodson et al., 2013.

claim: A number of swapped dimer structures have been solved from the eukaryotic Ser/Thr kinase class.

(2013) argued that these dimers are crystallographic artifacts (such as Chk2), our correlation between a domain-swapped dimer and its functional relevance would instead suggest that the reported structures are mechanistically meaningful.

claim: The functional effect of autophosphorylation is a 100-fold increase in the catalytic activity of Aurora A.

claim: Nature has evolved two distinct regulation mechanisms for Aurora A in different locations within the cell: autophosphorylation as activation in the centrosomes to promote phosphorylation of downstream targets, and TPX2-mediated activation at the spindle microtubules promoting Aurora A activity to another subset of downstream targets.
source: Our in vitro data together with previous in vivo results suggest that nature has evolved two distinct regulation mechanisms for Aurora A in different locations within the cell: autophosphorylation as activation in the centrosomes to promote phosphorylation of downstream targets, and TPX2-mediated activation at the spindle microtubules promoting Aurora A activity to another subset of downstream targets.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the study's findings and previous in vivo results.

claim: Aurora A kinase levels are available as early as S-phase and peak in the G2 phase.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the differential timing of Aurora A and TPX2 availability. Aurora A kinase levels are available as early as S-phase and peak in the G2 phase (Dutertre et al., 2002; Liu and Ruderman, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dutertre et al., 2002; Liu and Ruderman, 2006.

claim: TPX2 levels peak in the prometaphase/spindle formation stage that follows the G2 phase.

claim: The measured autophosphorylation kinetics is qualitatively in line with the progression of Aurora A T288 phosphorylation during the 3–4 h of G2/M duration in HeLa cells at 37°C.
source: In light of the increased local concentration of Aurora A in the centrosomes (Glover et al., 1995) (although the exact concentration is not known), our measured autophosphorylation kinetics is qualitatively in line with the progression of Aurora A T288 phosphorylation during the 3–4 h of G2/M duration in HeLa cells at 37°C (Crosio et al., 2002; Littlepage and Ruderman, 2002; Ohashi et al., 2006).
